title: The Peak-end Rule (How We Remember Purchases And Experiences)
description: We don’t remember experiences as a sum of every moment. Instead, we judge them based on two points: the most intense moment (the peak) and how they ended. This distorts our economic evaluations of services, vacations, and products.
shortDescription: We don’t remember experiences as a sum of every moment. Instead, we judge them based on two points: the most intense moment (the peak) and how they ended. This distorts our economic evaluations of services, vacations, and products.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We don’t remember experiences as a sum of every moment. Instead, we judge them based on two points: the most intense moment (the peak) and how they ended. This distorts our economic evaluations of services, vacations, and products.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A vacation with one incredible day and a smooth ending is remembered as “fantastic,” even if most days were mediocre and rainy.
A painful medical procedure that ends with a slightly less painful final minute is remembered as less painful overall, even if it lasted longer.
A restaurant meal: if the dessert is outstanding and the goodbye from the waiter is warm, you forget the average main course.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Rating an entire experience based on the highlight and the finish.
Returning to a brand because the last moment of the last interaction was positive, despite a history of problems.
Designing your own events to end on a high note, whether a party or a sales pitch.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “The ending made it all worth it.”
“It had its ups and downs, but overall it was amazing.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re choosing a repeat service because “it ended well” last time, while ignoring a pattern of mediocre performance.
You’re overpaying for an experience that is engineered to have a great peak and end, but the bulk is average.
You misremember the overall value of a long‑term investment because of a spectacular quarter or a terrible one.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Kahneman’s research on experienced utility shows that our remembering self dominates our decisions. The peak‑end rule is a cognitive shortcut that saves memory storage but discards duration. What matters is the highlight and the curtain call.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: When evaluating an experience, write down a daily rating to capture the whole arc, not just the peak and end.
If you’re designing an experience for others, invest disproportionately in the peak moment and the final touch.
For purchases, recall the middle of the ownership experience, not just the exciting start.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Planning a vacation that’s long and “nice” throughout, without a spectacular peak, and wondering why it felt forgettable.
Ignoring that a bad end can ruin the memory of a great experience.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A hotel chain spends heavily on a luxurious lobby and a warm farewell gift but keeps the rooms average. Guest reviews rave about the “amazing stay” because the peak (lobby awe) and end (farewell) are stellar, even though the sleep quality was mediocre.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: You don’t live your life in a highlight reel, but you remember it that way. Design your experiences so the peaks and the goodbye are worth the price of admission.
